summary:
Wetland Pulse tracks surface water in the northern Pantanal (Brazil), the world's largest tropical wetland, with NISAR L-band radar. 

Radar keeps measuring open water when clouds and wildfire smoke hide the ground from optical satellites. We turned eight NISAR GCOV acquisitions (July to October 2026) into a water-area time series and checked it against NASA OPERA water products and Sentinel-1 radar. 

The main result is detection: open water receded through the 2026 dry season (about -1 km² per day), and this trend stays negative under every threshold we tested. No single date falls outside the expected 95% range. 

As a secondary output, a Prophet model trained on three years of OPERA data projects the next four weeks as a relative change with its uncertainty, confirmed in direction by Sentinel-1. 

Everything is open: a public web map, the full pipeline, a data contract and an independent data review, so the method can move to other wetlands by editing one configuration file.
details:
What it does

Wetland Pulse measures how much open water the northern Pantanal has on each NISAR pass and shows it on an interactive map and chart. For each date, the map shows the radar image and the detected water. The chart shows the measured area, the range expected from the trend, the uncertainty of the method, and a short projection.


How it works

1. Water per date: NISAR L2 GCOV HH backscatter (track 132, frame 169) is speckle-filtered and converted to dB. Open water is every pixel darker than a fixed threshold (-16.75 dB, taken from the valley of the histogram), summed in km² over an 11,884 km² area.

2. Context and checks: NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS (2023-2026), OPERA RTC-S1 (Sentinel-1, 246 dates) and OPERA DSWx-S1 are reduced to the same per-date table. Cloudy scenes, wildfire smoke (2024) and burn scars that look like water in C-band are removed by explicit rules.

3. Detection: a Prophet trend on the NISAR series with a 95% band, repeated with the threshold at ±1 dB to show method uncertainty.

4. Projection: Prophet with yearly seasonality on three years of OPERA DSWx-HLS, reported as % change for the next four weeks with an 80% band, and checked against Sentinel-1.

5. Calibration gate: a source is converted to NISAR km² only if it beats a constant predictor. None did, so the projection stays in % and we say so.


Results

Open water fell from 376 km² (17 July) to 180-258 km² (August-October): about -1.0 km² per day, between -1.7 and -0.3 across thresholds. No date is outside the 95% range. NISAR and Sentinel-1 water maps agree on nearby dates (median F1 0.74). The November projection is stable (-1% to +1.5%, band about ±43%).


Benefits and impact

Fire brigades, water managers and researchers get a water signal that does not depend on clear skies. The pipeline, configuration and data contract are open, so the same method can follow other wetlands.


Tools

Python (numpy, scipy, scikit-image, h5py, rasterio, pandas, Prophet, earthaccess, asf_search), Leaflet, OpenStreetMap, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.


What makes it creative

Radar first, with optical and C-band radar as cross-checks instead of inputs. Every number ships with its uncertainty, and an AI-assisted but independent data review is part of the repository.


Factors we considered

NISAR GCOV is provisional and covers only the 2026 dry season. Water area depends on the threshold (±1 dB changes it by -37% to +56%). Our method maps open water only, not water under vegetation. Two NISAR dips (22 August, 27 September) are not confirmed by Sentinel-1. All limitations are listed on the site and in the README.
